q: what is via falsa in mastoidectomy
pos: Imaging case · Intracranial Hemorrhage Due to a Via Falsa › Intracranial Hemorrhage Due to a Via Falsa. Points to note: During mastoidectomy, drilling through the tegmen or the sinodural angle without recognising the middle fossa dura can enter the temporal lobe ('via falsa').
negs: Mastoid Surgery · Operating note › The case at a glance. Indications: Cholesteatoma of the attic or mastoid; chronic suppurative mastoiditis without cholesteatoma; acute coalescent mastoiditis, with or without temporal bone or intracranial complications; access for cochlear implantation, facial nerve surgery (decompression, tumour, grafting), endolymphatic sac surgery, labyrinthectomy, temporal bone resection and approaches to the posterior fossa and petrous apex

Mastoid Surgery · Operating note › The case at a glance. Canal wall up (intact): Drainage of acute mastoiditis; cholesteatoma that can be fully removed or will have a planned second look; implant and facial nerve surgery

Mastoid Surgery · Operating note › The case at a glance. Canal wall down: Small, sclerotic mastoid with limited exposure; low tegmen or forward sigmoid sinus; disease that cannot be fully removed and must be exteriorised; labyrinthine fistula; matrix on an eroded footplate or a widely dehiscent facial nerve; an only hearing ear; unreliable follow-up; revision surgery with higher risk

Mastoid Surgery · Operating note › The case at a glance. Contraindications: Unfit for general anaesthesia; poor wound healing; cholesteatoma extending beyond the temporal bone (mastoidectomy alone is inadequate). An auto-atticotomy or auto-mastoidectomy cavity may be managed by cleaning in clinic

Glomus Tumors · The operation: glomus jugulare › When to go canal wall down. For more exposure of tumour invading the carotid, or when the retrofacial and infralabyrinthine space is too tight (which may also mean transposing the facial nerve); the drum and ossicles can still be reconstructed.

q: protective function of the eustachian tube
pos: Eustachian tube · Anatomy atlas › Functions. Functions: Protection: the closed tube blocks nasopharyngeal sound and secretions (reflux); a cushion of air in the middle ear resists reflux.
negs: Eustachian tube disorders · Applied anatomy › The infant tube. Function approaches the adult pattern by about age seven to ten.
Eustachian tube disorders · Diagnosis › Tympanometry. Negative pressure or a flat curve; the inflation-deflation test assesses function through an intact or perforated drum.
Eustachian tube · Anatomy atlas › Functions. Functions: Ventilation: equalises middle ear pressure with the atmosphere and replaces absorbed gas.
Eustachian tube · Anatomy atlas › Functions. Functions: Normal tube opening needs an intact palate, working muscles and a non-inflamed lining.

Eustachian tube · Anatomy atlas › Functions. Clinical note: Patulous ET: the tube stays open (weight loss, pregnancy), causing autophony and hearing one's own breathing; symptoms ease when lying down.
Eustachian tube disorders · Applied anatomy › The infant tube. About half the adult length, nearly horizontal (about 10 degrees), wider, with floppy cartilage and little elastin.
Eustachian tube disorders · Applied anatomy › The infant tube. It refluxes nasopharyngeal secretions and protects the middle ear poorly, which explains the frequency of otitis media in children.
Eustachian tube · Anatomy atlas › Functions. Functions: Clearance: mucociliary and muscular drainage of middle ear secretions to the nasopharynx.
Eustachian tube disorders · Diagnosis › Other tests. Dye or saccharine clearance, sonotubometry, and endoscopy of the nasopharynx.
Eustachian tube disorders · Diagnosis › Other tests. The seven-item Eustachian Tube Dysfunction Questionnaire (ETDQ-7) is the standard symptom score.

Eustachian tube · Anatomy atlas › Eustachian tube dysfunction. Eustachian tube dysfunction: Obstructive (dilatory) dysfunction: the tube fails to open, giving aural fullness, muffled hearing, pain with pressure change, retraction and effusion.

Eustachian tube · Anatomy atlas › Eustachian tube dysfunction. Eustachian tube dysfunction: Causes include adenoids, rhinosinusitis, allergy, cleft palate (failure of tensor veli palatini) and nasopharyngeal tumours.

Eustachian tube · Anatomy atlas › Eustachian tube dysfunction. Eustachian tube dysfunction: Patulous tube: the tube stays open, so the patient hears their own voice and breathing (autophony); the drum moves with respiration.
